transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well, I suppose the main thing is… I can’t seem to turn the worrying off once it gets going. I’ll tell myself, “All right, I’ve made the list, I checked the dates, I’ve done what can reasonably be done,” and still my mind just keeps circling back to it. It’s like I know, logically, that I’ve handled things as much as I can, but that doesn’t make the worry stop. It just keeps running in the background, and sometimes right in the foreground, honestly.
Do you find yourself worrying about many different parts of your life, rather than mainly one specific problem?

Yes, definitely. It isn’t just one thing, like… if it were only one bill or one medical appointment or something, I could almost understand it. But my mind sort of wanders from one concern to the next. I’ll be thinking about the exhibition schedule and whether everything is lined up properly, and then somehow I’m thinking about my daughter’s travel plans, whether she’ll make connections safely, whether something will go wrong, and then I’ll notice the weather and think, oh, the gutters on the house probably need attention, and what if that turns into damage, and then that becomes a whole other thread.

It’s not always enormous things at first. Sometimes it starts with something fairly ordinary, but in my head it begins to feel like it could unravel into something much bigger if I don’t stay on top of it. So yes, it’s many different parts of life, not just one specific problem.
Do you find yourself repeatedly checking things because of these worries, even after you already know they’re taken care of?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that, because I don’t think of myself as doing a lot of, you know, ritual-type checking. I mean, I might look back at something once or twice if I’m unsure, like a date or whether I wrote something down correctly, but I don’t know that I repeatedly check things over and over after I truly know they’re handled.

It’s more that the thought keeps coming back in my mind. So even if something is technically taken care of, I may still keep thinking, “But what if I missed something?” I don’t always go and check again, though. Sometimes I just sit with that uneasy feeling and go over it mentally, which is frustrating in its own way.
Did these worries start after a particular stressful event or major life change?

Yes… I think it did, at least that’s when I really noticed it becoming this constant thing. It’s been about seven months now. My friend died, and shortly after that I was trying to keep our projects moving, sort of not let everything fall apart or disappear, and I think that’s when the worrying started to take up much more space in my head.

At first I thought, well, of course I’m unsettled, there was a lot going on and it mattered to me. But then it just didn’t really settle back down. Even after the immediate things were handled, my mind stayed in that mode of trying to anticipate every possible problem. So yes, I’d say it began shortly after her death and everything I was trying to keep going afterward.
When the worrying starts, do you find it hard to control or stop it?

Yes… that’s really the part that made me feel like I should come in, honestly. Once the worrying gets started, I can’t seem to turn it off. I’ll try to be reasonable with myself — I’ll say, “All right, you’ve made the list, you checked the dates, you’ve done what you can do for now.” And for a few moments that helps, but then the thought sort of circles back around.

It feels like my mind doesn’t accept that things are handled. I can know, logically, that I’ve done all I reasonably can, but there’s still this feeling of, “What if there’s something I forgot?” or “What if I haven’t thought far enough ahead?” And then I’m back in it again. I don’t mean to keep going over it, but it’s hard to stop once it catches hold.
Do you often feel physically tense or keyed up when you’re worrying?

Yes, I do. Not always in some dramatic way, but I notice it in my body more than I’d like. I’ll be sitting in my own living room, where there’s really no reason to feel on edge, and I feel sort of wound up, like I can’t quite settle into the chair.

If I’m on the phone about something even mildly stressful, I’ll catch myself tapping my fingers, or shifting around, or standing up when I don’t need to. Sometimes I get up and straighten a pillow or move papers around, not because it actually matters, but because just sitting quietly with the worry makes me feel jumpy. It’s like my body wants to be doing something, even if there isn’t really anything useful to do.
Have these worries been happening on most days for at least six months?

Yes… yes, I’d say most days. It’s been about seven months now, since shortly after my friend died and I was trying to keep those projects moving. I remember thinking at the beginning that it was just the situation, that once things were more settled I’d feel more like myself again.

But it didn’t really ease off in that way. It became almost part of the rhythm of my days, if that makes sense — not every single minute, but most days there’s been something my mind latches onto and turns over. So yes, it has definitely been longer than six months.
Are your worries mostly about your friend’s death and the projects connected to it, rather than about lots of unrelated parts of life?

No, not only those things. That’s where it seemed to start, or at least that’s the clearest thread I can point to, but it hasn’t stayed neatly in that box.

My mind kind of roams from one thing to the next. One minute I’m thinking about the exhibition schedule and whether something will fall through there, and then somehow I’m thinking about my daughter’s travel plans and whether she’ll get delayed or something will go wrong, and then I’ll notice the rain and start wondering whether the gutters on the house need fixing. And then that doesn’t feel like just gutters, it starts to feel like, well, if I ignore it maybe there’ll be water damage, and then repairs, and then a whole expensive mess.

So it’s not only about my friend’s death or the projects connected to it. Those are part of it, definitely, but the worry seems to spread. Small things don’t stay small in my head lately. They start to feel as if they could unravel into something much bigger.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that. I mean, I do sleep, so it’s not as if I’m up all night pacing the house or anything like that. But I haven’t really been keeping track of it in a careful way.

Some nights I notice I’m not settling down as easily, but then other nights I think I’m probably sleeping more or less normally. It’s hard for me to separate what’s actually “trouble sleeping” from just being 67 and waking up sometimes, or having an active mind at bedtime. I wouldn’t want to overstate it.

So… I guess I’d say I haven’t clearly noticed a major sleep problem, but I’m not entirely sure.
Do you often feel easily tired?

Yes, I do. More than I would expect, really. It’s not dramatic like I’m collapsing or anything, but I feel worn out very easily.

Even on nights when I think I’ve slept all the way through, I can wake up feeling as though I’ve already put in half a day before I’ve even properly started. And then I’ll do something ordinary — water the garden beds, or sort through papers for book club, something that shouldn’t be a major undertaking — and afterward I find I need to sit down and just gather myself.

It’s a bit frustrating, because these are not strenuous things. They’re the normal little tasks of my day. But lately they seem to take more out of me than they used to.
Has this worrying been interfering with your daily life?

Yes, I think it has, though maybe not in a completely obvious way from the outside. I’m still doing the things I normally do. I still keep up with the garden, and I still go to book club, so it’s not as if everything has stopped. But I can tell I’m not quite managing things the way I used to.

With book club, for example, I’ll arrive having read less carefully than I meant to, or I’ll feel as though I’m sort of catching up while I’m there rather than coming in with my thoughts organized. And with the exhibition planning, I’ve started turning down pieces of it — not the whole thing, but certain parts — because they feel harder to manage than they should. Even things that used to feel manageable now seem to require this extra mental effort.

So yes, it is interfering some. Not catastrophically, but enough that I notice I’m pulling back in places and not feeling as prepared or capable as I normally would.
Do you feel your worrying is mainly a reaction to your friend’s death and its aftermath, or does it now feel separate from that event?

I think it began very much as a reaction to my friend’s death, yes. At least, that’s when I first remember it taking hold in this more persistent way. It was shortly after she died, and I was trying to keep our projects moving — things we had both cared about — and at first I told myself, well, of course I’m unsettled, of course I’m worried, there’s been a loss and now there are all these loose ends.

But it’s been about seven months now, and I suppose that’s what makes me hesitate. It still feels connected to her death in some ways, because that was the start of it, but it doesn’t feel only like a direct reaction anymore. It’s more as if the worrying got started then and has just continued on, attaching itself to the projects and responsibilities and whether I’m handling things properly. So yes, it started after she died, but now it feels like it has carried on past the immediate aftermath.
Do you feel your level of worry is more than the situation actually calls for?

Yes… I think it probably is more than the situation calls for, though I don’t always recognize that in the moment.

It’s not that there’s nothing real to think about — there are schedules to keep straight, and family things, and the house always has something that needs attention. But my mind doesn’t seem to just consider them and put them aside. It roams from one thing to the next. I’ll be thinking about the exhibition schedule, and then suddenly I’m worrying about my daughter’s travel plans, and then I’m thinking, “Oh, what about the gutters on the house, did I ever have those looked at properly?” And each thing starts to feel as if, if I don’t stay on top of it immediately, it could somehow unravel into something much bigger.

When I say it out loud, I can hear that some of it is probably out of proportion. A gutter repair is a gutter repair. A travel plan is usually just a travel plan. But in my head, it can feel like one missed detail will set off a whole chain of problems. So yes, I do think the level of worry is more than the actual situation calls for.
Has this ongoing worrying lasted longer than six months after your friend died?

Yes, it has. It’s been about seven months now, if I’m counting from shortly after my friend died. That was when I first noticed it becoming this ongoing thing, especially when I was trying to keep our projects going without her.

At first I thought, well, of course I’m worried, there’s been a lot to manage. But it hasn’t really let up in the way I expected it might. So yes, it has lasted longer than six months.
Have you been finding it hard to concentrate?

I’m not entirely sure how to answer that. I mean, I haven’t especially thought of it as “trouble concentrating,” if that makes sense. I do find my mind can wander when I’m trying to settle on one thing, but I’m not sure whether that’s the same as not being able to concentrate.

If I’m reading something, for example, I might have to go back over a paragraph because I realize I was thinking about something else, but I don’t know that I’d say it’s severe or that I absolutely can’t focus. It’s more that my attention gets pulled around. But no, I wouldn’t say I’ve clearly noticed a major concentration problem, at least not in a way I’ve been keeping track of.
Have you been more irritable than usual?

I don’t know that I’d say I’ve been more irritable, exactly. I mean, I have moments where I feel a bit short with things, or I suppose I get annoyed when there are too many small things piling up at once, but I’m not sure that’s very different from how I’ve always been.

I haven’t had people telling me I’m snapping at them or anything like that. At least, not that I can think of. Sometimes I may sound sharper than I intend, and then I think afterward, “Oh, that probably came out more tense than I meant it.” But I wouldn’t say I’ve clearly noticed a big increase in irritability. It’s more… I’m aware I can feel wound up, but I’m not sure that turns into being irritable with other people in any consistent way.
Even now, does the worrying feel present in your life regardless of reminders of your friend’s death?

Yes… yes, I think it does. It isn’t only when something specifically reminds me of her or of what happened. That can bring things up, of course, but the worrying has sort of taken on a life of its own now.

My mind will just keep roaming from one thing to another — the exhibition schedule, then my daughter’s travel plans, then whether the house gutters need fixing — and none of those things are necessarily huge on their own. But in my head they start to feel as if they could unravel into something much bigger if I don’t stay on top of them. So even on an ordinary day, with no obvious reminder, it’s still there in the background.
Do you worry on most days even when there isn’t any particular problem happening?

Yes, I think I do. It’s not always because something has actually gone wrong that day. Sometimes there isn’t any clear problem at all, and yet my mind just starts moving from one thing to the next.

I’ll be thinking about the exhibition schedule, and then suddenly I’m thinking about my daughter’s travel plans, and then it’s the house gutters, and whether I’ve left that too long, and then one small thing seems to connect to another. None of it is necessarily disastrous on its own, but it starts to feel as if, if I don’t keep watching everything, something could unravel into a much bigger problem. So yes… most days there’s some version of that going on, even if nothing particular has happened.
Have you been having muscle tension?

Yes, I think so. I hadn’t really thought of it as a symptom, exactly, but by the evening my shoulders and neck can feel terribly tight, like I’ve been holding myself stiff all day without noticing.

I’ll be sitting down trying to read, or going over plans for the garden center activities, and suddenly I realize my jaw is clenched, or my shoulders are practically up by my ears. Then I try to drop them and relax, but a few minutes later I catch myself doing it again. It’s not dramatic, but it’s this constant braced feeling, especially toward the end of the day.

It still feels connected to her death in some ways, because that was the start of it, but it doesn’t feel only like a direct reaction anymore. It’s more as if the worrying got started then and has just continued on, attaching itself to the projects and responsibilities and whether I’m handling things properly. So yes, it started after she died, but now it feels like it has carried on past the immediate aftermath.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the worry is excessive relative to the actual stressor, which helps distinguish generalized anxiety disorder from an adjustment disorder related to bereavement.
doctor.question: Do you feel your level of worry is more than the situation actually calls for?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: My mind keeps roaming from the exhibition schedule to my daughter's travel plans to whether the house gutters need fixing, and small things start to feel as if they could unravel into something much bigger.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether the amount of worry is disproportionate to the actual situation, which directly relates to excessive anxiety and worry.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think it probably is more than the situation calls for, though I don’t always recognize that in the moment.

It’s not that there’s nothing real to think about — there are schedules to keep straight, and family things, and the house always has something that needs attention. But my mind doesn’t seem to just consider them and put them aside. It roams from one thing to the next. I’ll be thinking about the exhibition schedule, and then suddenly I’m worrying about my daughter’s travel plans, and then I’m thinking, “Oh, what about the gutters on the house, did I ever have those looked at properly?” And each thing starts to feel as if, if I don’t stay on top of it immediately, it could somehow unravel into something much bigger.

When I say it out loud, I can hear that some of it is probably out of proportion. A gutter repair is a gutter repair. A travel plan is usually just a travel plan. But in my head, it can feel like one missed detail will set off a whole chain of problems. So yes, I do think the level of worry is more than the actual situation calls for.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the anxiety has persisted beyond the 6-month limit for adjustment disorder, which best distinguishes generalized anxiety disorder from adjustment disorder at this point.
doctor.question: Has this ongoing worrying lasted longer than six months after your friend died?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about seven months, since shortly after my friend died and I tried to keep our projects moving.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the worrying has persisted for longer than six months after the friend’s death, which directly concerns the duration of symptoms.

patient.answer:
Yes, it has. It’s been about seven months now, if I’m counting from shortly after my friend died. That was when I first noticed it becoming this ongoing thing, especially when I was trying to keep our projects going without her.

At first I thought, well, of course I’m worried, there’s been a lot to manage. But it hasn’t really let up in the way I expected it might. So yes, it has lasted longer than six months.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the anxiety is accompanied by another core GAD symptom to better distinguish generalized anxiety disorder from adjustment disorder or unspecified anxiety disorder.
doctor.question: Have you been finding it hard to concentrate?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty concentrating, but the provided symptom profile does not include a concentration-related symptom item.

patient.answer:
I’m not entirely sure how to answer that. I mean, I haven’t especially thought of it as “trouble concentrating,” if that makes sense. I do find my mind can wander when I’m trying to settle on one thing, but I’m not sure whether that’s the same as not being able to concentrate.

If I’m reading something, for example, I might have to go back over a paragraph because I realize I was thinking about something else, but I don’t know that I’d say it’s severe or that I absolutely can’t focus. It’s more that my attention gets pulled around. But no, I wouldn’t say I’ve clearly noticed a major concentration problem, at least not in a way I’ve been keeping track of.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are additional core GAD symptoms to strengthen differentiation from adjustment disorder, focusing on irritability as one of the remaining DSM-5 associated symptoms.
doctor.question: Have you been more irritable than usual?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about irritability, but the provided symptom profile does not include an irritability symptom item.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I’d say I’ve been more irritable, exactly. I mean, I have moments where I feel a bit short with things, or I suppose I get annoyed when there are too many small things piling up at once, but I’m not sure that’s very different from how I’ve always been.

I haven’t had people telling me I’m snapping at them or anything like that. At least, not that I can think of. Sometimes I may sound sharper than I intend, and then I think afterward, “Oh, that probably came out more tense than I meant it.” But I wouldn’t say I’ve clearly noticed a big increase in irritability. It’s more… I’m aware I can feel wound up, but I’m not sure that turns into being irritable with other people in any consistent way.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has persistent anxiety and worry occurring across domains independent of the original stressor, which most strongly distinguishes generalized anxiety disorder from adjustment disorder with anxiety.
doctor.question: Even now, does the worrying feel present in your life regardless of reminders of your friend’s death?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: My mind keeps roaming from the exhibition schedule to my daughter's travel plans to whether the house gutters need fixing, and small things start to feel as if they could unravel into something much bigger.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether the worry is ongoing across life generally and not only triggered by reminders of the friend’s death, which directly concerns persistent excessive worry about multiple events or activities.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, I think it does. It isn’t only when something specifically reminds me of her or of what happened. That can bring things up, of course, but the worrying has sort of taken on a life of its own now.

My mind will just keep roaming from one thing to another — the exhibition schedule, then my daughter’s travel plans, then whether the house gutters need fixing — and none of those things are necessarily huge on their own. But in my head they start to feel as if they could unravel into something much bigger if I don’t stay on top of them. So even on an ordinary day, with no obvious reminder, it’s still there in the background.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the worry is excessive and pervasive enough to meet another core GAD criterion versus a nonspecific anxiety reaction.
doctor.question: Do you worry on most days even when there isn’t any particular problem happening?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: My mind keeps roaming from the exhibition schedule to my daughter's travel plans to whether the house gutters need fixing, and small things start to feel as if they could unravel into something much bigger.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether worry occurs on most days even without a current specific problem, which directly assesses persistent excessive anxiety and worry.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think I do. It’s not always because something has actually gone wrong that day. Sometimes there isn’t any clear problem at all, and yet my mind just starts moving from one thing to the next.

I’ll be thinking about the exhibition schedule, and then suddenly I’m thinking about my daughter’s travel plans, and then it’s the house gutters, and whether I’ve left that too long, and then one small thing seems to connect to another. None of it is necessarily disastrous on its own, but it starts to feel as if, if I don’t keep watching everything, something could unravel into a much bigger problem. So yes… most days there’s some version of that going on, even if nothing particular has happened.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the worry is accompanied by clinically significant muscle tension, which would further support generalized anxiety disorder over adjustment disorder or unspecified anxiety disorder.
doctor.question: Have you been having muscle tension?

target_item.name: Muscle_Tension
target_item.manifestation: By evening my shoulders and neck are so tight from holding myself braced all day that I catch myself clenching my jaw while I read or plan the garden center activities.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about muscle tension.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think so. I hadn’t really thought of it as a symptom, exactly, but by the evening my shoulders and neck can feel terribly tight, like I’ve been holding myself stiff all day without noticing.

I’ll be sitting down trying to read, or going over plans for the garden center activities, and suddenly I realize my jaw is clenched, or my shoulders are practically up by my ears. Then I try to drop them and relax, but a few minutes later I catch myself doing it again. It’s not dramatic, but it’s this constant braced feeling, especially toward the end of the day.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes excessive anxiety and worry about multiple domains of life, occurring on most days for about seven months, with clear difficulty controlling the worry. Associated symptoms confirmed include feeling keyed up/restless, easy fatigability, and muscle tension, with functional interference in reading, book club participation, and exhibition planning. Although onset followed a psychosocial stressor (friend's death), the worry has generalized beyond that event and persisted beyond the immediate aftermath, making generalized anxiety disorder more fitting than adjustment disorder or unspecified anxiety disorder.
